Dried Yak Cheese

Served at: Losar (Tibetan New Year)

Makes about 1 pound (450 g) of dried cheesePrep 30 minCook 12 hours (drying time)

Dried Yak Cheese, known as chhurpi in Tibetan culture, is a traditional cheese made from yak milk. It is a staple during Losar, the Tibetan New Year, symbolizing strength and endurance for the year ahead. This cheese is often enjoyed as a snack or used in various festive dishes.

Ingredients

  • 1 gallon (3.8 liters) fresh yak milk or whole cow’s milk
  • 1/4 teaspoon rennet or 2 tablespoons plain yogurt (as a starter culture)
  • Salt to taste

Method

  1. Heat the milk gently in a large pot until it reaches about 86°F (30°C).
  2. Add the rennet or yogurt to the milk and stir gently to combine.
  3. Allow the milk to sit undisturbed for 6-12 hours at room temperature until it curdles and separates into curds and whey.
  4. Once curds form, cut them into small cubes using a knife.
  5. Gently heat the curds to about 104°F (40°C) while stirring slowly to help them firm up.
  6. Drain the whey by pouring the curds into a cheesecloth-lined colander.
  7. Gather the cheesecloth and press out excess whey by applying weight or squeezing gently.
  8. Add salt to the curds and mix well to taste.
  9. Shape the curds into flat, thick discs or blocks.
  10. Place the shaped cheese on a clean surface in a well-ventilated, dry area away from direct sunlight.
  11. Allow the cheese to dry and harden for 12 hours to several days depending on humidity, turning occasionally to ensure even drying.
  12. Once fully dried and hard, the cheese is ready to be stored or served.

Tips

  • Use fresh, high-quality milk for the best flavor and texture.
  • If yak milk is unavailable, whole cow’s milk is a suitable substitute.
  • Store dried yak cheese in an airtight container in a cool, dry place to preserve it for months.
